usamts-1999-r1-01.title: Narrow down the digits of a
usamts-1999-r1-01.body:
We have $b = 3a$ and $c = 5a$, all three-digit numbers.

* **Hundreds digit of $a$.** $c = 5a < 1000$ forces $a < 200$, so $a$ starts with 1.
* **Units digit of $a$.** If it is even, $c = 5a$ ends in 0 — not allowed. If it is 5, then $b$ and $c$ also end in 5 — a repeat. If it is 1, it repeats the leading 1; if it is 7, then $b = 3a$ ends in 1 — a repeat. So $a$ ends in 3 or 9, and $c$ ends in 5.
* **Ends in 3:** $a = 1x3$. Since $5 \cdot 3 = 15$, the tens digit of $c$ is the last digit of $5x + 1$, which is 1 (a repeat) when $x$ is even. So $x$ is odd: $x \ne 1, 3$ (repeats), $x \ne 9$ ($b = 3a$ ends in 9), $x \ne 5$ ($b = 459$ repeats 5). That leaves $x = 7$: $a = 173$, $b = 519$ — repeats 1. No solution.
* **Ends in 9:** $a = 1x9$, $c = 5a$ ends in 5 and $c < 1000$ needs $a \le 199$. Trying $x = 2, 3, \dots, 8$ (with $x \ne 1, 5, 9$):
  * $129 \to 387, 645$: digits $1,2,9,3,8,7,6,4,5$ — all different ✓
  * $139 \to 417$ (repeat 1), $149 \to 447$ (repeat 4), $159$ (repeats 5 in $c = 795$), $169 \to 507$ (contains 0), $179 \to 537, 895$ (repeat 9), $189 \to 945$ (repeat 9).

So the unique answer is $a = 129$, $b = 387$, $c = 645$.

**Answer: $a = 129$, $b = 387$, $c = 645$**

usamts-1999-r1-02.title: Repunits
usamts-1999-r1-02.body:
Let $R = \underbrace{11\ldots1}_{1999} = \frac{10^{1999} - 1}{9}$. The digits of $N$ are $R$ shifted left by 1999 places plus $2R$:
$$N = R\cdot 10^{1999} + 2R = R\,(10^{1999} + 2).$$
(Small case: $111222 = 111\cdot 1002$.)

Next, $10^{1999} + 2 = 2\,(5\cdot 10^{1998} + 1)$. The number $5\cdot10^{1998} + 1 = 500\ldots01$ has digit sum 6, so it is divisible by 3, and
$$\frac{5\cdot 10^{1998} + 1}{3} = 1\underbrace{66\ldots6}_{1997}7$$
(compare $51 = 3\cdot 17$, $501 = 3\cdot 167$, $5001 = 3\cdot 1667$). In general $3 \cdot 1\underbrace{6\ldots6}_{k-1}7 = 5\underbrace{0\ldots0}_{k-1}1$, by long multiplication: $3\cdot 7 = 21$ (write 1, carry 2), each $3 \cdot 6 + 2 = 20$ (write 0, carry 2), and finally $3\cdot 1 + 2 = 5$.

Therefore
$$N = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot \underbrace{11\ldots1}_{1999} \cdot 1\underbrace{66\ldots6}_{1997}7,$$
a product of four integers greater than 1.

*(Other factorizations exist; e.g. one can check with Fermat's little theorem that 23 also divides $5\cdot 10^{1998} + 1$.)*

usamts-1999-r1-03.title: Midpoints and an equilateral triangle
usamts-1999-r1-03.body:
Take $BC = 1$, $AC = \sqrt3$, $AB = 2$. A triangle is similar to $ABC$ with one quarter of the area exactly when it is a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle with hypotenuse $1$ (ratio $\frac12$, area ratio $\frac14$), i.e. with sides $\frac12, \frac{\sqrt3}2, 1$.

Let $D$, $E$, $F$ be the midpoints of $AB$, $BC$, $CA$. By the midline theorem $DE \parallel AC$ and $DF \parallel BC$, so $DE \perp BC$, $DF \perp AC$, and $DECF$ is a rectangle with $DE = FC = \frac{\sqrt3}2$, $DF = EC = \frac12$. Also $DA = DB = DC = 1$ (the midpoint of the hypotenuse is the circumcenter), so triangle $DBC$ is equilateral with side 1 and triangle $DAC$ is isosceles with $\angle DAC = \angle DCA = 30^\circ$.

**Way 1.** Pieces $DBE$, $ADF$, $DEC$, $DFC$ (rectangle $DECF$ cut along diagonal $DC$).
* $DBE$: right angle at $E$, $\angle B = 60^\circ$, hypotenuse $DB = 1$. ✓
* $ADF$: right angle at $F$, $\angle A = 30^\circ$, hypotenuse $AD = 1$. ✓
* $DEC$ and $DFC$: right angles at $E$ and $F$, legs $\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and $\frac12$, hypotenuse $DC = 1$. ✓

**Way 2.** Pieces $DBE$, $ADF$, $EDF$, $ECF$ (rectangle cut along the other diagonal $EF$). The two rectangle halves have right angles at $D$ and $C$ and legs $\frac{\sqrt3}2$, $\frac12$, so they are again $30$-$60$-$90$ triangles with hypotenuse 1. ✓

**Ways 3 and 4.** Keep $ADF$ and $CDF$ (the isosceles triangle $ADC$ cut by its axis $DF$ — two $30$-$60$-$90$ triangles with hypotenuses $DA = DC = 1$). Cut the equilateral triangle $DBC$ by its altitude **from $B$** (to the midpoint of $DC$) in Way 3, or by its altitude **from $C$** (to the midpoint $G$ of $DB$) in Way 4. An altitude of an equilateral triangle of side 1 splits it into two $30$-$60$-$90$ triangles with hypotenuse 1. ✓ (The altitude from $D$ is $DE$, which gives Way 1 again.)

In each way the four pieces cover $ABC$ without overlap, and each is similar to $ABC$ with ratio $\frac12$, hence area $\frac14$ of $ABC$. ∎

usamts-1999-r1-04.title: Count layers, then use a regular tetrahedron
usamts-1999-r1-04.body:
**Number of layers.** Layer $i$ has the triangular number $\frac{i(i+1)}2$ of balls, and
$$\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{i(i+1)}{2} = \frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6} = \binom{n+2}{3}.$$
We need $n(n+1)(n+2) = 6\cdot 8436 = 50616 = 36\cdot 37\cdot 38$, so $n = 36$ layers.

**Height of the centers.** The centers of the four corner balls form a regular tetrahedron. Along an edge there are 36 balls whose centers are 2 cm apart, so the edge is $35\cdot 2 = 70$ cm.

The height of a regular tetrahedron with edge $s$: the foot of the altitude is the center of the base triangle, at distance $\frac{s}{\sqrt3}$ from each base vertex, so the height is
$$\sqrt{s^2 - \frac{s^2}{3}} = s\sqrt{\tfrac23} = \frac{s\sqrt6}{3}.$$
With $s = 70$: $\frac{70\sqrt6}{3}$.

**Height of the pile.** Add the radius above the top center and below the bottom centers: $1 + 1 = 2$ cm. So the height is
$$2 + \frac{70\sqrt6}{3} \approx 59.15 \text{ cm}.$$

**Answer: $2 + \frac{70\sqrt6}{3}$ cm**

usamts-1999-r1-04.title: Layer by layer
usamts-1999-r1-04.body: Four mutually touching balls have centers forming a regular tetrahedron of edge 2, whose height is $\frac{2\sqrt6}{3}$. Each layer's centers sit exactly this much higher than the layer below (each ball rests in a pocket formed by three balls under it). With 36 layers (since $\binom{38}{3} = 8436$), the top center is $35\cdot\frac{2\sqrt6}3 = \frac{70\sqrt6}3$ above the bottom centers, and adding the two radii gives $2 + \frac{70\sqrt6}{3}$ cm.

usamts-1999-r1-05.title: Vectors
usamts-1999-r1-05.body:
Use position vectors. Then $F = \frac{A + B}2$, $H = \frac{C + D}2$, so
$$X = \frac{F + H}2 = \frac{A + B + C + D}{4},\qquad Y = \frac{G + I}{2} = \frac{B + C + D + E}{4}.$$
Hence $Y - X = \frac{E - A}{4}$, i.e.
$$XY = \frac{AE}{4}.$$
$AE$ is one of $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$, and $XY = AE/4$ is an integer only for $AE = 4$ (giving $XY = 1$). This value really occurs: a convex pentagon with sides $1, 2, 3, 5, 4$ in order (so $EA = 4$) exists, since each length is less than the sum of the others.

**Answer: $AE = 4$**

usamts-1999-r1-05.title: Midlines
usamts-1999-r1-05.body:
Let $Z$ be the midpoint of $BE$. In triangle $BCD$, $GH$ is a midline: $GH \parallel BD$, $GH = \frac{BD}2$. In triangle $BED$, $ZI$ is a midline: $ZI \parallel BD$, $ZI = \frac{BD}2$. So $GHIZ$ is a parallelogram, and its diagonals $GI$ and $HZ$ bisect each other: $Y$ is the midpoint of $HZ$.

Now in triangle $HFZ$, $X$ and $Y$ are midpoints of $HF$ and $HZ$, so $XY = \frac{FZ}2$. In triangle $BAE$, $F$ and $Z$ are midpoints of $BA$ and $BE$, so $FZ = \frac{AE}{2}$. Therefore $XY = \frac{AE}4$, and as before $AE = 4$.

**Answer: 4**
